seoDescription: Learn the fundamentals of unit testing with JUnit and why mocking with Mockito simplifies isolated tests. This tutorial shows how to set up a Maven project, write a simple Calculator class and JUnit test cases, run assertions, use setup/teardown annotations, and explains the need for mocking external services (APIs, databases) to speed tests and avoid dependencies. Ideal for Java developers adopting automated tests and test-driven thinking.

chapters.title: Introduction and Maven project setup
chapters.description: Introduces the topic and creates a Maven quickstart project prepared to use JUnit and Mockito dependencies.

chapters.title: Why unit testing matters
chapters.description: Explains the purpose of unit tests, testing individual classes and methods, and introduces TDD.

chapters.title: Creating a simple Calculator class
chapters.description: Builds a minimal Calculator class with an add method to serve as the unit to test.

chapters.title: Creating a JUnit test case
chapters.description: Shows how to add a test class in the test folder, use annotations, and prepare to assert results.

chapters.title: Assertions and running tests
chapters.description: Demonstrates assertEquals usage, running a JUnit test, and interpreting green (pass) and red (fail) results.

chapters.title: Setup and teardown annotations
chapters.description: Covers using @Before and @After to initialize and release resources for tests.

chapters.title: Why mocking is necessary
chapters.description: Introduces a CalculatorService interface and explains problems when unit tests depend on external services like cloud APIs or databases.

chapters.title: Mocking frameworks and conclusion
chapters.description: Explains mocking as creating fake services, distinguishes mock/stub/fake, and lists mocking frameworks like Mockito, ending with a preview of the next video.

chapters.title: Closing silence
chapters.description: Video runtime padding with no additional speech.

summary:
## Key Concepts

- **JUnit**: a Java unit testing framework used to automate testing of classes and methods; helps validate behavior with assertions such as **assertEquals**.

- **Unit**: the smallest testable part of an application (typically a method or class); unit tests isolate and verify unit behavior.

- **Test-driven development (TDD)**: write tests before implementation; tests initially fail, then pass after implementation.

- **Automation**: run thousands of tests automatically instead of manual verification to detect regressions quickly.

- **@Before / @After**: lifecycle annotations to set up and tear down resources (e.g., create objects in a setup method, release in teardown).

- **Mocking**: create fake implementations of dependencies (APIs, databases, external services) so unit tests run fast and remain deterministic.

- **Mock vs Stub vs Fake**: related but different concepts; mocks simulate behavior for testing interactions, while stubs/fakes provide simplified implementations. (Detailed distinctions promised in a follow-up.)

- **Mocking frameworks**: examples include **JMock**, **EasyMock**, and **Mockito**; Mockito is highlighted as an easy-to-use option.

> [!TIP] Use JUnit for fast, automated verification of your units and add mocks for external dependencies to keep tests isolated and fast.

> [!NOTE] Keep test names and folders organized (e.g., TestCalculator) and use static imports for assertion readability.

> [!IMPORTANT] Do not rely on external services in unit tests — mock them to avoid slow, flaky tests and to focus on the unit under test.

## Introduction and Maven project setup

Welcome back, aliens. My name is David Reddy, and in this video we're going to talk about what is JUnit and why do we need Mockito. In fact, if you have been in Java for a long time you might have heard about JUnit, right? Or maybe you have worked on JUnit and you might have heard about Mockito. So what exactly Mockito is and why do we need it? So we'll start the example with JUnit and let's move towards why do we need Mockito. Again, in this video we are going to not talk about how to use Mockito but why to use Mockito; in the next video we're going to talk about how to use Mockito. So what we will do is let's get a sample project and while doing that let me just create a Maven project. Of course now it is a Maven project because I need those two dependencies which is JUnit and Mockito. So let's go for Maven project. I will say I will need a simple quick start project. I don't need any web application and will give an artifact id as a project name. We'll say this is demo JUnit again with Mockito, of course, but then let's not have a big big name here and let's click on finish.

## Why unit testing matters

Now once we got our project in this area you can see we have other projects as well. Let's ignore that; let's focus only on our project which is demo JUnit. Now what we will do is first, let's try to understand why do we need a testing or test framework. If you know that's great. If you don't know, what happens is whenever you make a project, in your project there will be lots of classes, right? Especially if you're working in Java, so you will be having lots of classes and in each class you'll be having some methods. Now what happens is when you build an application you have to make sure that you also test an application. How do you test it? So one way is you can build the complete application and you can test it, but you know it is not that flexible to test the entire application. If something goes wrong, how would you know what went wrong? So what we do is we test the individual units. What is a unit? The smallest part of your application. Now in terms of Java classes and methods they are what you say the smallest part, right? So methods have a behavior, right? So you're testing that behavior. So what we will do is we will test the classes and the methods. That is called unit. Using JUnit you can do that. You can achieve unit testing in Java using JUnit. Again, there are lots of other testing frameworks available but then we will be using JUnit here. Luckily, if we talk about a Maven project, if you expand your Maven dependency you can see by default we have JUnit, so we don't have to worry about that. So what we will do now, how do we actually implement that? There's one more concept which you should know is TDD, which is test-driven development. Normally what happens is when we make a project and we test it, right? Another approach is before baking a module, create a test case. It's something like you have not built a thing, but then before building that stuff you have to test it. You have to get a test case. Of course your test case will fail, right? Because if you are testing something which is not there, of course it will fail. Then you have to create a module which should work, right, then it will pass. So first your test case will fail and later it will pass.

## Creating a simple Calculator class

But again let's not get into that way because this video will be long if I go in that way. So let's create a very simple class here to test. I will not be using any complicated stuff here. Let's say I'm using a Calculator. I love this example of Calculator for every example because I believe you know let's make it as simple as possible, right? So let's use Calculator. And of course when I say Calculator you will be having some basic features. Every Calculator will have a method which is addition. So what we will do is we'll say public int add(int i, int j) and this is your add method which returns i plus j. Now how do you test it? Of course you can call this, right, so from your main method. In your app you have your main method so what you can do is create an object of Calculator and call add method. Your job is done, right? But that is not how you actually test because that is manual testing. If you are checking by your hand it is manual. Let's automate it because you might have thousands of classes in your application, right? And if you change one class it may affect other classes as well. Can you test all the thousand classes manually? That's not possible, right? Even if it is possible it is not flexible. So let's automate this stuff. What happens is even if you change one class it should test all the classes and for that we need automation and of course for that we can use JUnit.

## Creating a JUnit test case

So how do you test this Calculator? What we can do is in your test package — if you can see we have a main folder here and we have a test folder — in this test folder let me create a test case. When you right-click and say JUnit test case it is there. In case it is not available... so it's available; let's click on this and I will name this test case by naming convention; we should have TestCalculator because you are testing this Calculator, right? So it's TestCalculator. I will click on finish. Okay, so we got this test case. But normally, okay let's not use this extent where there are multiple ways of doing this. We can use annotation way, right? So let's use annotations here just to make our work simple. What I will do here is I want to test the add method, right? So we should get a test case. I will say public void testAdd. Now how do you test it? Okay, so what we need is to test the Calculator object. First we need an object of Calculator; that's how we test it, right? So we'll say Calculator c = new Calculator. But normally what we do is, okay, let's just have this Calculator there and here what we will do is we'll say okay how do you test it. Now to test a Calculator we need to assert test because we are testing a method, right? So this is your first test case. But as you can see we are getting some issue. I guess the problem is it is with the version of JUnit. So let's use the latest JUnit. How do I get the latest? I will go to Maven repository and I will search for JUnit because we want the latest one. Okay let's search for JUnit and let's pick up 4.11. Let's go back to our pom file because this is where you will change the version, right? So I will just go to the pom file and let's use the latest one. Let's remove the dependency and let's put the new one. Okay, and now once we got a new dependency you can see now we got that annotation available. So in your Maven dependency as well you can see we have JUnit. Now let's say control-space and let's import JUnit. Here how do you test it now? So in this we have something called assertEquals. Now assertEquals is a static method of the Assert class. Let's use static import because every time you have to say Assert.assertEquals that doesn't make sense, right? So let's use the static import.

## Assertions and running tests

Now assertEquals will take two parameters: the first one is expected, the second one is actual. So I will go for actual first. When I call c.add by passing two values, two and three, it should return five. So I'm expecting five. If your logic is right, of course this test will pass. Now how do you test it? Do we have to run it as a normal Java application? No, because we're testing it. Right-click here and say Run As — it's giving the option of JUnit Test. I will click on generate test. The amazing part is when you say run you're running one test only and one test passed and you can see a green symbol there. This green line means your test passed. And that's the beauty. Let's say if I make a mistake. Let's say in Calculator, and normally this is not the case — we will not make a mistake in Calculator — but let's say by mistake you are saying i + j + 1. That's a mistake. Now if you test it and run this test once again you can see we got a red line, which means your test fails. Your expected value was five and because of some coding issue or logical algorithm problem you have made a mistake here and the test fails. Now you know something went wrong. Let's again do some modification; you realize that we should not have one there. So this is the right logic and again you will test and you can see we got green. This is JUnit. Again, this is the simplest example you can think of.

## Setup and teardown annotations

In fact in JUnit we have Before and After. Now why do we need Before? Let's say the object which I've created here is an open object. Let's say if you want to define and create an instance inside a method, normally we create that method something like setup. So we say setup because this is a method where you will create all the objects. Something like initially this will be null and later you can say c = new Calculator. But then when to call this? You can say Before. So Before will be called before test, and you can also have After. If you want to remove or release some resources you can do that. Right. This is JUnit. Okay, so this is perfect. Even if you have thousand classes we can test all the classes using JUnit. Okay, so that makes sense. But why do we need Mockito? This is JUnit, right? Simple. Again, this is not a complete session; I just wanted to show you why do we need Mockito.

## Why mocking is necessary

Okay, now why do we need Mockito here? Let's think about it. Let's say we have a Calculator and by some means I don't know why but let's say we have one more class and that class is CalculatorService, or maybe CalculatorService is an interface. In this interface you actually have a method called add, public int add(int i, int j). Now you will think, okay why do we need this? Just think about it: this is a simple application right, calculator, and that's why you're defining it. But sometimes you might want to process this information using a cloud service. Let's say if you have a cloud server and that cloud server says, hey programmer, if you want to add two numbers you don't have to do that by yourself, you can use our cloud service. So every time a user clicks on the calculate button your application will connect with the server and you will get the response. Second scenario is you're fetching this data from a database. Maybe this CalculatorService is not a calculator server; this is something you will connect with database. Now what will happen is every time you test this Calculator, because this CalculatorService is well tested — whoever has built this service, maybe Google, have done proper testing on CalculatorService — as a developer of this application I don't need to test CalculatorService, right? I need to test only Calculator. But the problem is every time you test Calculator it will be using this CalculatorService. So just imagine every time you test it, let's say if you are building an application and in your application you have thousands of classes; if you make one change since you're using JUnit it will test all the classes and even if five classes interact with the cloud service, even if five classes interact with database, five classes interacting with something else — just imagine if you are testing the application, if you're running the tests it will take 10 minutes to run. Will it make sense? Of course not. Right? And why do we need to test the service? We have to test our application, right?

## Mocking frameworks and conclusion

So what normally we do is we create a stub because without the real implementation we cannot make it work. Sometimes your application depends on some other application or maybe your class is dependent on some other class object. That other class object may be working with a database or it may not even be built; how can you test it? That's where we have to mock those services. When I say mock, it simply means that we can create a fake service. It is not the actual service. Every time we test this Calculator it will not connect with the server; we will test this Calculator with the help of a fake service or a mock service. Again there's a big difference between mock, fake, and stub; we'll talk about that in one of the videos. But then we create a mock service. What it means: this is not the actual service; this is a duplicate copy of your service so that you don't have to worry about the actual service. You have to only test your Calculator. That's where we need mocking frameworks. You can do mocking with the help of mocking frameworks and there are different mocking frameworks available. We have JMock, we have EasyMock, and we have Mockito. Mockito is one of the easiest mocking libraries available. In the next video we're going to talk about how do you use mocking, I mean how do you do mocking in this application. So yeah, that's it. This is the simplest application where we have talked about JUnit, how to build a JUnit test case, and why do we need Mockito. I hope you enjoyed this video.
